screens.title: Malware Analysis & Reverse Engineering Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will gain a working understanding of how analysts examine malicious binaries to determine intent and extract indicators of compromise. We begin by distinguishing two complementary approaches: static analysis, which inspects files without running them, and dynamic analysis, which observes real behavior inside a controlled environment. You will learn why both approaches are necessary: static work is safe and fast for initial triage, while dynamic testing reveals runtime actions that static methods miss, especially when malware is packed or obfuscated. I will also guide you through setting up a safe, isolated virtual machine with snapshots and simulated network services so you can execute samples without risking your host or network. Practical tool knowledge is essential: string extractors, disassemblers, dependency viewers, process and A P I monitors, network captures, and debuggers are all part of the analyst’s toolkit. Throughout, we focus on producing actionable outputs — hashes, C2 domains, registry changes, and file paths — that feed SIEMs and EDR systems. As you go through the screens, notice how each step reduces uncertainty about a sample’s behavior. By the end you should be able to plan a simple static and dynamic workflow, extract meaningful IoCs, and know when to escalate to deeper reverse engineering.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map the practical skills you need to analyze malware safely and effectively. First, you will learn to differentiate static and dynamic analysis. That skill matters because it tells you which techniques reveal observable artifacts without execution and which reveal runtime behaviors only visible during execution. Second, you will set up and configure a safe, isolated VM environment with snapshots and simulated network services; the goal is to run samples without risking production networks while capturing meaningful network artifacts. Third, you will use common static analysis tools — string extractors, dependency viewers, and disassemblers — to form an initial hypothesis about a sample’s capabilities. Finally, you will perform dynamic analysis to observe process activity, file and registry changes, A P I calls, and network communications, and then translate those observations into actionable indicators. Each objective includes a concrete action and a reason why it matters in incident response. Expect to practice these skills through example workflows that convert raw files into IoCs for SIEM and EDR ingestion.

screens.title: Static vs Dynamic Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Static and dynamic analysis are complementary ways to inspect malware. Static analysis inspects a binary without running it. You extract printable strings, inspect headers and import tables, and run disassemblers to read assembly or decompiled pseudo-code. This approach is safe and fast and often yields immediate clues such as file type, imported libraries, and hard-coded URLs. A concrete example: string extraction might reveal a ransom note filename or a hard-coded domain used for command and control. A common misconception is that static analysis alone is sufficient; sophisticated malware often uses packing or encryption to hide strings and imports, which static methods cannot easily bypass. Dynamic analysis executes the sample in a controlled environment to observe real behavior: created files, modified registry keys, spawned processes, injected code, and actual network traffic. For example, a packed sample may unpack itself in memory and reveal decrypted strings and C2 domains only during runtime. A risk is accidental infection if isolation is insufficient. The takeaway: use static methods first to triage safely, then move to dynamic testing in a properly isolated VM to confirm behavior and collect concrete IoCs. Which artifacts from each approach will you prioritize for incident response?

keyIdea.title: Static vs Dynamic
keyIdea.text: Static for safe triage and quick clues; dynamic for definitive behavior and IoC generation under isolation.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Static vs Dynamic
Core Concept

Static vs Dynamic Analysis

Compare what each approach reveals, their benefits, and their blind spots.

Static — Safe triage
  • Extract strings and imports to form initial hypotheses.
  • Use disassemblers to inspect code paths without execution.
  • Limitations: packers and encryption hide runtime artifacts.
Dynamic — Observe runtime
  • Execute in an isolated VM to see real behavior.
  • Capture file/registry changes, process injections, and network traffic.
  • Risk: poor isolation can lead to infection of host or network.
Key Takeaway

Start with static triage for safety. Use dynamic analysis to confirm behavior and extract final IoCs in an isolated lab.

Concrete Example: Packed Ransomware
Strings are encrypted in the file, so static tools show little. When executed in a VM, the sample unpacks in memory and reveals a ransom note filename and C2 domain.
Common Mistake
Running a suspicious sample on a non-isolated machine or skipping static triage before execution risks loss of forensic evidence and broader infection.
Pro Tip
Always snapshot a clean VM state before execution. Use simulated network services to capture C2 behavior safely.

screens.title: Preparing a Safe, Isolated Analysis Environment
screens.narratorSegment: A proper analysis environment starts with isolation and repeatability. First, use a virtual machine on a host that is not connected to corporate networks. The VM must be segregated and, by default, disconnected from the internet. Take a clean snapshot before any execution so you can revert immediately after analysis. Second, install monitoring tools such as Process Monitor, Process Explorer, and Wireshark inside the VM to capture runtime actions. Third, use network simulation tools like FakeNet or INetSim if you need to observe C2 behavior without allowing real connections. Fake service responses help you see how the malware reacts while preventing real communications. Fourth, limit clipboard and shared folders between host and guest to reduce escape vectors. A concrete example: before running a suspected ransomware executable, create a snapshot, place a set of dummy files to observe encryption, start Process Monitor and Wireshark, and enable FakeNet to catch any attempted domains. A common misconception is that a single snapshot suffices; in practice, take separate snapshots for different test variations and always verify isolation settings. The takeaway: predictable, snapshot-backed VMs with simulated network services let you execute samples safely and collect the forensic artifacts you need.

keyIdea.title: Environment essentials
keyIdea.text: Isolation, snapshots, monitoring tools, and simulated network services are required to run malware safely and capture reliable evidence.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Safe Environment
Process Flow

Isolated VM Setup

Step 1 — Create clean VM and snapshot
Install OS, apply no corporate network connections, and take a baseline snapshot to revert after each run.
Step 2 — Install monitoring
Process Monitor/Explorer, Wireshark, API monitoring, and debuggers inside the VM capture the runtime activity.
Step 3 — Configure network simulation
Use FakeNet-NG or INetSim to answer DNS and HTTP requests so malware cannot reach real C2 servers.
Key Takeaway

Multiple snapshots and simulated network responses allow safe experimentation and repeatable evidence collection.

Checklist: Before execution
  • Confirm VM network isolation and snapshot saved.
  • Start Process Monitor and Wireshark captures.
  • Enable FakeNet/INetSim if network observation is required.
  • Place benign test files to detect encryption or modification.
Common Mistake
Leaving shared folders or host integration enabled can allow malware to escape the VM. Disable these features before running samples.
Try This
Create a snapshot, then intentionally modify a test file after running a sample. Revert to confirm snapshot integrity.

screens.title: Static Analysis Tools and Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: Static analysis begins with tools that reveal file structure and embedded data without execution. File type identification tools tell you whether a sample is a Portable Executable or an ELF and may flag known packers. String extractors like the basic strings utility or FLOSS reveal printable ASCII and Unicode text embedded in binaries. These strings often include filenames, URLs, error messages, or A P I names that indicate behavior. Dependency viewers show which DLLs an executable imports; for example, imports from ws2_32. dll indicate networking capability, while advapi32. dll suggests registry or cryptography use. Disassemblers like Ghidra or IDA Pro translate machine code into assembly and often provide pseudo-code that helps you find functions of interest. A concrete example: running strings on a suspected ransomware binary might reveal a ransom note filename or a Bitcoin address fragment. A common misconception is to treat string hits as definitive proof; attackers often encrypt strings or use A P I hashing to hide intent. So combine string and import analysis with disassembly to confirm hypotheses. Document the artifacts you find and prioritize items that can be turned into IoCs, such as domains, file paths, and specific A P I calls.

keyIdea.text: Use file-ID, strings, dependency viewers, and disassemblers to form and validate hypotheses without running the sample.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Static Tools
Definition

Key static techniques

File type identification
Use file or PEiD to confirm format and detect packers before deeper analysis.
String extraction
Extract printable text with strings or FLOSS to locate potential URLs, file names, and API references.
Dependency analysis
Inspect import tables to understand high-level capabilities like networking or crypto.
Key Takeaway

Static tools give safe, quick clues. Treat findings as hypotheses to confirm with dynamic or reverse-engineering steps.

Example: Strings Output
> strings invoice.exe
RANSOM_NOTE.txt
Bitcoin: 1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa
CreateFileW
WriteFile
ws2_32.dll
http://malicious.example/update
This output suggests a ransom note, networking, and file manipulation — useful leads for triage.
Common Mistake
Assuming strings are always meaningful. Attackers encrypt strings; use disassembly to confirm if strings are decoded at runtime.

screens.title: Disassemblers and Decompilers
screens.narratorSegment: Disassemblers and decompilers convert machine code into assembly or higher-level pseudo-code so you can reason about a program’s logic. Ghidra and IDA Pro provide an interactive view of functions, control flow, and imported APIs. When you open a Portable Executable in one of these tools, examine the import table for functions such as CreateRemoteThread, WriteFile, or InternetOpenUrl — these indicate code injection, file operations, and network activity respectively. Use the call graph and function cross references to find where suspicious imports are used. A concrete example: you may see a function that calls CreateFile followed by WriteFile and then deletes the original; that pattern suggests dropping a payload or modifying files. A common misconception is that decompiler output is perfectly accurate; it is an approximation and must be validated against assembly and dynamic behavior. For packed or obfuscated binaries, disassemblers help identify unpacking routines and the original entry point. The practical tip: label functions, document offsets of interest, and export the import list and function names to feed into your incident report or IoC list. Disassemblers and Decompilers means use imports and call graphs to prioritize functions for dynamic inspection and breakpoint placement in a debugger.. In practical terms, ghidra, ida pro and reading import tables to find interesting functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Disassemblers
Tool Overview

Reading imports & functions

Identify functions of interest by their imported APIs, then explore cross-references and call graphs to see how those APIs are used.
What to look for
  • CreateRemoteThread, WriteFile, InternetOpenUrl as red flags.
  • Call graphs showing network or file routines used widely.
  • Strings decoded at runtime or large blocks used for configuration.
Pro Tip
Label discovered functions and export an import list for documentation. Use these labels to set debugger breakpoints later.
Key Takeaway

Imports and function references guide your reverse-engineering focus and aid breakpoint placement during dynamic analysis.

Concrete Scenario
You find a function that resolves a domain, opens an HTTP connection, then writes to disk. This indicates network-assisted payload retrieval. Mark these points for API monitoring and network capture in the VM.
Common Mistake
Over-trusting decompiler output. Always cross-check pseudo-code against assembly and runtime behavior before forming conclusions.

screens.title: Dynamic Analysis: Observing Processes, Files, and Registry
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic analysis makes invisible behavior visible. Begin by capturing process activity with Process Monitor or Process Explorer to record process creation, termination, and parent-child relationships. Look for suspicious parentage such as a document reader spawning a command shell, or a legitimate process being injected into. Record file system activity to detect dropped payloads, new file extensions, or modifications to user data. Registry monitoring is equally important: malware often persists via Run keys or service entries, and registry changes can indicate configuration storage. A concrete workflow: start Process Monitor with filters for the sample's process name, execute the sample, and then examine entries for file creations with write operations and registry sets under Run keys. A common misconception is to rely solely on timestamps; ensure you correlate process activity with network captures and snapshots. Document the exact file paths, registry keys, and process names observed — these are host-based IoCs. The takeaway is that Process Monitor provides a timeline of host changes that, when combined with network data, create a fuller picture of the malware’s capabilities and persistence strategies. What host artifacts will you prioritize when feeding alerts to your SIEM?

keyIdea.text: Process and registry logs reveal persistence and file changes that are critical IoCs for host-based detection.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Process & Registry
Process Flow

Capturing host activity

Use Process Monitor to log process creation, file writes, and registry modifications to identify persistence and payload behavior.
What to capture
  • Process launches, parent PID, and injected processes.
  • File creates/renames and deleted originals.
  • Registry Run keys, service entries, and configuration keys.
Pro Tip
Filter Process Monitor to the suspect process to reduce noise and preserve a clear timeline for post-execution analysis.
Key Takeaway

Host logs reveal persistence mechanisms and file activity that feed EDR and incident response actions.

Concrete Example
After execution, Process Monitor shows invoice.exe creating README.txt, renaming user documents with a new extension, and adding a Run key for persistence. These exact artifacts become host-based IoCs.
Common Mistake
Not correlating host activity timestamps with network captures can obscure the sequence of events. Always sync clocks and captures before analysis.

screens.title: Network Analysis: Wireshark and FakeNet
screens.narratorSegment: Network captures are essential for identifying command and control activity and data exfiltration attempts. Wireshark captures packets and lets you inspect protocols, reconstruct streams, and extract payload data. But allowing malware to reach the internet is dangerous, so pair captures with FakeNet or INetSim. FakeNet simulates DNS, HTTP, and common services and responds to malware requests so you can see intended C2 domains without contacting real infrastructure. For example, if a sample tries to beacon to attacker. example, FakeNet will answer and log the attempt while Wireshark records the packets, enabling you to reconstruct what the malware sent or requested. A common contrast: FakeNet gives you safe, controlled responses; Wireshark gives you the raw bytes for forensic reconstruction. Misconception to avoid: believing that no network traffic equals no network capability. Malware may delay or attempt to detect sandboxing; if you see DNS lookups or failed connections, that’s still valuable. The takeaway: combine simulated services and packet capture to produce network-based IoCs such as domains, IPs, user agents, and distinctive protocol patterns that your defenders can use. Network Analysis: Wireshark and FakeNet means use fakenet to contain c2 and wireshark to capture packet-level evidence that yields network iocs and protocol details.. In practical terms, capturing traffic and simulating services to contain c2 interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Network Analysis
Definition

Capture and simulate

Run Wireshark to record traffic and FakeNet to safely answer network requests so malware cannot reach real C2 servers.
What to capture
  • DNS queries and responses for domain discovery.
  • HTTP requests and headers for user-agent and payload data.
  • Unusual protocols or encrypted tunnels that suggest data exfiltration.
Pro Tip
Capture both simulated responses and raw packets. FakeNet shows intent; Wireshark gives forensics you can extract and decode.
Key Takeaway

Simulate network services to contain risk and use packet captures to extract network IoCs for detection.

Concrete Example
FakeNet responds to an HTTP POST. Wireshark shows the POST payload contains a base64 blob that decodes to configuration data and C2 commands. These domain and payload patterns become network IoCs.
Common Mistake
Not running simulated services when the malware expects real responses. If fake services are absent, the sample may exit or hide its behavior.

screens.title: API Monitoring and Sandboxes
screens.narratorSegment: A P I monitoring records the sequence of system calls malware makes, providing a detailed trace of behavior that static tools can miss. Tools like A P I Monitor log calls to CreateFile, WriteFile, RegSetValue, and networking APIs, giving you an ordered list of operations and their parameters. Sandboxes such as Cuckoo automate many dynamic tasks: they execute the sample inside an isolated environment, capture process, file, registry, and network activity, and produce a consolidated report. A concrete example: A P I Monitor shows a call to RegSetValue under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with the malware path; Cuckoo’s report correlates this with a NetBIOS scan and outgoing HTTP connections, suggesting a persistence plus lateral-reconnaissance capability. A common misconception is that sandbox reports are exhaustive — automated sandboxes may miss nuanced behavior or be detected by the sample and evaded. Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › API & Sandbox
Tool Demonstration

API Monitor and Cuckoo

API logs and sandbox reports complement each other. Use API monitoring to validate sandbox findings and collect parameter-level details.
API log sample
> RegSetValueExW(HKEY_CURRENT_USER, 'Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run', 'Invoice', 'C:\\Temp\\invoice.exe')
> CreateFileW('C:\\Users\\Public\\doc1.docx', GENERIC_WRITE)
Key Takeaway

API-level detail confirms exact parameters and sequences of operations that are critical for accurate detection rules.

Sandbox Caveat
Automated sandboxes can be detected and evaded. Use sandbox output as a primer, then perform manual observation for confirmation.
Practical Step
Run Cuckoo for a first pass, export process and network reports, then attach API Monitor for parameter-level traces in subsequent manual runs.

screens.title: Reverse Engineering with a Debugger
screens.narratorSegment: Reverse engineering with a debugger is essential when static analysis is blocked by packers or obfuscation. A debugger lets you run the binary step-by-step, inspect memory, set breakpoints, and modify registers to follow the unpacking routine until the original entry point, or OEP, is revealed. For example, set breakpoints on memory allocation and execution transfer functions, then step until you observe decrypted code written to executable memory. A concrete example: a sample may allocate memory, decrypt a payload into that space, and then create a thread to execute it. By breaking on CreateThread or VirtualProtect calls, you can intercept the unpacked code and dump it for static analysis. A common misconception is that debugging is only for experts; with practice, breakpoint strategies and memory inspection become systematic techniques. The practical outcome is that debugging produces an unpacked binary or a memory dump that disassemblers can analyze more effectively. The closing question: when you encounter an unknown packer, which A P I breakpoints and memory inspection steps will you use first to reveal runtime code? Reverse Engineering with a Debugger means use breakpoints on thread creation and memory protection changes to catch runtime unpacking and extract the original code for analysis.. In practical terms, using x64dbg, ollydbg, or gdb to step through unpacking and find the oep. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Debugger
Definition

Debugger-based reverse engineering

Step through execution to uncover unpacking routines and reveal the original, executable code in memory.
Breakpoint strategy
  • Break on CreateThread, VirtualAlloc, VirtualProtect, and LoadLibrary.
  • Inspect memory regions for newly written executable pages.
  • Dump memory once unpacked and analyze in a disassembler.
Key Takeaway

Debugging uncovers runtime-decrypted code and is the primary method to defeat packing and obfuscation for analysis.

Concrete Example
Break on VirtualProtect. Step to the point where the process marks memory as executable. Dump that memory and open it in Ghidra to see deobfuscated code and meaningful function names.
Common Mistake
Rushing to dump memory without noting the instruction pointer and module offsets can create misaligned dumps that are hard to analyze. Record offsets and context carefully.

screens.title: IoC Extraction and Reporting
screens.narratorSegment: The end goal of analysis is actionable intelligence. After static and dynamic steps, gather host and network indicators: file hashes, dropped file paths, new registry keys, mutex names, C2 domains and IPs, and distinctive network headers or payload patterns. Prioritize artifacts that are stable and unique, like SHA256 hashes and exact registry values, rather than ephemeral elements like temporary filenames that may vary. A concrete example: if you observe invoice. exe creating README. txt and contacting bad. example on port 8080 while writing files with the ". locked" extension, report the SHA256 hash of the executable, the domain bad. example, and the file extension as correlated IoCs. Document the context: the exact command line, the timestamp, the monitored A P I calls, and the Process Monitor entries that show the registry keys altered. A common misconception is that more indicators are always better; noisy or generic IoCs produce false positives. The practical rule: prefer precise, reproducible artifacts and include enough context so a detection engineer can implement reliable rules in a SIEM or EDR. The final question: which three IoCs will you prioritize from a ransomware run and why?

Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › IoC Extraction
Practice Workflow

Collecting and prioritizing IoCs

Gather hashes, network indicators, file paths, registry keys, and mutexes, then provide contextual evidence for each item.
Recommended priorities
  • SHA256 and other file hashes for exact identification.
  • C2 domains/IPs and specific URLs observed in network captures.
  • Registry keys used for persistence and file extensions of encrypted files.
Pro Tip
Include sample Process Monitor lines or Wireshark packet excerpts to help detection engineers reproduce detection logic.
Key Takeaway

Actionable IoCs are precise, reproducible, and accompanied by context so they can be deployed reliably in detection systems.

Example Report Snippet
SHA256: <hash> — Created README.txt at C:\\Users\\Public\\README.txt — Contacted bad.example on 198.51.100.23:8080 — Created Run key at HKCU\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run
Common Mistake
Publishing noisy indicators without context results in detection rules that trigger on benign behavior. Always provide supporting evidence with IoCs.

screens.title: Invoice.exe: Static and Dynamic Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario demonstrates a repeatable workflow for an executable named invoice. exe. Start with static analysis: run file or PEiD to confirm it's a PE file and check for packers. Compute SHA256 for reporting. Run strings or FLOSS to extract readable artifacts and inspect the import table for networking or file APIs. These steps produce initial hypotheses — for instance, strings referencing README or imports from ws2_32. dll suggest file and network activity. Next, prepare your isolated VM: take a snapshot, enable FakeNet, and start Process Monitor and Wireshark. Place benign documents and images on the desktop to observe encryption behavior. Execute invoice. exe and watch for file renames, newly created ransom notes, and registry Run key changes. Capture DNS and HTTP attempts with Wireshark and check FakeNet logs for attempted domains. If the binary is packed, attach a debugger and set breakpoints on VirtualProtect and CreateThread to find unpacked code, dump it, and analyze in Ghidra. Finally, extract IoCs: file hashes, observed domains, created registry keys, and any unique file extensions. A common mistake is rushing to upload samples to public sandboxes; keep samples within your isolated lab and document each step for reproducibility. After this workflow, ask yourself which three indicators you would prioritize to protect your environment.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Invoice.exe Workflow
Hands-on Activity

Static → Dynamic → IoC

Follow a conservative, repeatable workflow: triage statically, prepare an isolated VM, execute with monitors, and extract IoCs.
Static steps
  • File/PE identification and SHA256 hashing.
  • Run strings/FLOSS and document suspicious strings.
  • Inspect import table for ws2_32, advapi32, kernel32 indicators.
Dynamic steps
  • Snapshot VM, enable FakeNet, start Process Monitor and Wireshark.
  • Execute sample, capture file, registry, process, and network events.
  • Record and export captures and logs for reporting.
Key Takeaway

A documented, repeatable workflow produces reliable IoCs and preserves evidence for incident response.

Example IoCs to extract
  • SHA256 of invoice.exe and any dropped payloads.
  • Observed C2 domains or IP addresses and ports.
  • Created registry Run keys and modified file extensions used for encryption.
Common Mistake
Uploading sensitive samples to public sandboxes can leak data and expose your environment. Keep all handling inside your isolated lab.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember

Use these concepts together: static triage informs your dynamic plan, dynamic observation feeds reverse-engineering efforts when needed, and all findings must be documented as actionable IoCs. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will gain a working understanding of how analysts examine malicious binaries to determine intent and extract indicators of compromise. We begin by distinguishing two complementary approaches: static analysis, which inspects files without running them, and dynamic analysis, which observes real behavior inside a controlled environment. You will learn why both approaches are necessary: static work is safe and fast for initial triage, while dynamic testing reveals runtime actions that static methods miss, especially when malware is packed or obfuscated. I will also guide you through setting up a safe, isolated virtual machine with snapshots and simulated network services so you can execute samples without risking your host or network. Practical tool knowledge is essential: string extractors, disassemblers, dependency viewers, process and A P I monitors, network captures, and debuggers are all part of the analyst’s toolkit. Throughout, we focus on producing actionable outputs — hashes, C2 domains, registry changes, and file paths — that feed SIEMs and EDR systems. As you go through the screens, notice how each step reduces uncertainty about a sample’s behavior. By the end you should be able to plan a simple static and dynamic workflow, extract meaningful IoCs, and know when to escalate to deeper reverse engineering.

These objectives map the practical skills you need to analyze malware safely and effectively. First, you will learn to differentiate static and dynamic analysis. That skill matters because it tells you which techniques reveal observable artifacts without execution and which reveal runtime behaviors only visible during execution. Second, you will set up and configure a safe, isolated VM environment with snapshots and simulated network services; the goal is to run samples without risking production networks while capturing meaningful network artifacts. Third, you will use common static analysis tools — string extractors, dependency viewers, and disassemblers — to form an initial hypothesis about a sample’s capabilities. Finally, you will perform dynamic analysis to observe process activity, file and registry changes, A P I calls, and network communications, and then translate those observations into actionable indicators. Each objective includes a concrete action and a reason why it matters in incident response. Expect to practice these skills through example workflows that convert raw files into IoCs for SIEM and EDR ingestion.

Continuing the objectives, we emphasize measurable outcomes: you should be able to select tools to reveal packers or obfuscation, use a debugger to step through an unpacking routine, and document findings so they can be used in detection rules. This includes generating file hashes, capturing C2 domains or IPs, identifying persistence registry modifications, and listing dropped files or created mutexes. These outcomes are essential because raw observations are only useful when documented and converted to indicators that security controls can consume. The lesson stresses common mistakes like running samples on production machines or skipping static analysis before execution. You will be asked to demonstrate competency by outlining a three-step static analysis plan, configuring a snapshot-based VM, and extracting at least three IoCs from a controlled run. Practice and repeatability are key; every time you run a sample, you should be able to reproduce your steps and results so your team can respond efficiently.

Static and dynamic analysis are complementary ways to inspect malware. Static analysis inspects a binary without running it. You extract printable strings, inspect headers and import tables, and run disassemblers to read assembly or decompiled pseudo-code. This approach is safe and fast and often yields immediate clues such as file type, imported libraries, and hard-coded URLs. A concrete example: string extraction might reveal a ransom note filename or a hard-coded domain used for command and control. A common misconception is that static analysis alone is sufficient; sophisticated malware often uses packing or encryption to hide strings and imports, which static methods cannot easily bypass. Dynamic analysis executes the sample in a controlled environment to observe real behavior: created files, modified registry keys, spawned processes, injected code, and actual network traffic. For example, a packed sample may unpack itself in memory and reveal decrypted strings and C2 domains only during runtime. A risk is accidental infection if isolation is insufficient. The takeaway: use static methods first to triage safely, then move to dynamic testing in a properly isolated VM to confirm behavior and collect concrete IoCs. Which artifacts from each approach will you prioritize for incident response?

A proper analysis environment starts with isolation and repeatability. First, use a virtual machine on a host that is not connected to corporate networks. The VM must be segregated and, by default, disconnected from the internet. Take a clean snapshot before any execution so you can revert immediately after analysis. Second, install monitoring tools such as Process Monitor, Process Explorer, and Wireshark inside the VM to capture runtime actions. Third, use network simulation tools like FakeNet or INetSim if you need to observe C2 behavior without allowing real connections. Fake service responses help you see how the malware reacts while preventing real communications. Fourth, limit clipboard and shared folders between host and guest to reduce escape vectors. A concrete example: before running a suspected ransomware executable, create a snapshot, place a set of dummy files to observe encryption, start Process Monitor and Wireshark, and enable FakeNet to catch any attempted domains. A common misconception is that a single snapshot suffices; in practice, take separate snapshots for different test variations and always verify isolation settings. The takeaway: predictable, snapshot-backed VMs with simulated network services let you execute samples safely and collect the forensic artifacts you need.

Static analysis begins with tools that reveal file structure and embedded data without execution. File type identification tools tell you whether a sample is a Portable Executable or an ELF and may flag known packers. String extractors like the basic strings utility or FLOSS reveal printable ASCII and Unicode text embedded in binaries. These strings often include filenames, URLs, error messages, or A P I names that indicate behavior. Dependency viewers show which DLLs an executable imports; for example, imports from ws2_32. dll indicate networking capability, while advapi32. dll suggests registry or cryptography use. Disassemblers like Ghidra or IDA Pro translate machine code into assembly and often provide pseudo-code that helps you find functions of interest. A concrete example: running strings on a suspected ransomware binary might reveal a ransom note filename or a Bitcoin address fragment. A common misconception is to treat string hits as definitive proof; attackers often encrypt strings or use A P I hashing to hide intent. So combine string and import analysis with disassembly to confirm hypotheses. Document the artifacts you find and prioritize items that can be turned into IoCs, such as domains, file paths, and specific A P I calls.

Disassemblers and decompilers convert machine code into assembly or higher-level pseudo-code so you can reason about a program’s logic. Ghidra and IDA Pro provide an interactive view of functions, control flow, and imported APIs. When you open a Portable Executable in one of these tools, examine the import table for functions such as CreateRemoteThread, WriteFile, or InternetOpenUrl — these indicate code injection, file operations, and network activity respectively. Use the call graph and function cross references to find where suspicious imports are used. A concrete example: you may see a function that calls CreateFile followed by WriteFile and then deletes the original; that pattern suggests dropping a payload or modifying files. A common misconception is that decompiler output is perfectly accurate; it is an approximation and must be validated against assembly and dynamic behavior. For packed or obfuscated binaries, disassemblers help identify unpacking routines and the original entry point. The practical tip: label functions, document offsets of interest, and export the import list and function names to feed into your incident report or IoC list. Disassemblers and Decompilers means use imports and call graphs to prioritize functions for dynamic inspection and breakpoint placement in a debugger.. In practical terms, ghidra, ida pro and reading import tables to find interesting functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dynamic analysis makes invisible behavior visible. Begin by capturing process activity with Process Monitor or Process Explorer to record process creation, termination, and parent-child relationships. Look for suspicious parentage such as a document reader spawning a command shell, or a legitimate process being injected into. Record file system activity to detect dropped payloads, new file extensions, or modifications to user data. Registry monitoring is equally important: malware often persists via Run keys or service entries, and registry changes can indicate configuration storage. A concrete workflow: start Process Monitor with filters for the sample's process name, execute the sample, and then examine entries for file creations with write operations and registry sets under Run keys. A common misconception is to rely solely on timestamps; ensure you correlate process activity with network captures and snapshots. Document the exact file paths, registry keys, and process names observed — these are host-based IoCs. The takeaway is that Process Monitor provides a timeline of host changes that, when combined with network data, create a fuller picture of the malware’s capabilities and persistence strategies. What host artifacts will you prioritize when feeding alerts to your SIEM?

Network captures are essential for identifying command and control activity and data exfiltration attempts. Wireshark captures packets and lets you inspect protocols, reconstruct streams, and extract payload data. But allowing malware to reach the internet is dangerous, so pair captures with FakeNet or INetSim. FakeNet simulates DNS, HTTP, and common services and responds to malware requests so you can see intended C2 domains without contacting real infrastructure. For example, if a sample tries to beacon to attacker. example, FakeNet will answer and log the attempt while Wireshark records the packets, enabling you to reconstruct what the malware sent or requested. A common contrast: FakeNet gives you safe, controlled responses; Wireshark gives you the raw bytes for forensic reconstruction. Misconception to avoid: believing that no network traffic equals no network capability. Malware may delay or attempt to detect sandboxing; if you see DNS lookups or failed connections, that’s still valuable. The takeaway: combine simulated services and packet capture to produce network-based IoCs such as domains, IPs, user agents, and distinctive protocol patterns that your defenders can use. These concise concepts capture the essential ideas you should remember when performing malware analysis. First, static analysis inspects files without execution to gather quick clues like strings and imports; it’s safe but can be thwarted by packing or encryption. Second, dynamic analysis executes samples in an isolated VM to observe file, registry, process, and network behavior; it reveals runtime actions but must be done with strict isolation. Third, reverse engineering with disassemblers and debuggers uncovers obfuscated logic and runtime-decrypted code, allowing you to extract detailed indicators and understand attacker techniques. Use these concepts together: static triage informs your dynamic plan, dynamic observation feeds reverse-engineering efforts when needed, and all findings must be documented as actionable IoCs.
